title: Kernels, PCA, K-means, and GMM
summary: Connect geometry, dimensionality reduction, and mixture modeling instead of memorizing them as separate algorithms.
objectives: Interpret a kernel as an inner product in a feature space

sections.title: Lecture core · Three different questions
sections.body: PCA asks for a low-dimensional linear view that preserves variance. K-means asks which centroid is closest under squared Euclidean distance. GMM asks which latent component plausibly generated the point and returns a probability, not just a label.

teaching.concept: A fitted model can be judged by representation, estimation, or optimization questions; these are different failure diagnoses.
teaching.useWhen: Use the distinction when two models have similar training loss but differ in stability, capacity, or convergence.
teaching.examMove: Ask first whether the function is representable, then whether finite data identify it, then whether the algorithm found the intended solution.
teaching.trap: Improving the optimizer cannot repair a hypothesis class that excludes the target.

sections.title: Lecture core · Kernel idea
sections.body: A kernel lets us compute inner products after an implicit feature map without explicitly constructing every transformed coordinate. The useful mental model is geometry in a richer space; the kernel choice controls which notion of similarity is available.

teaching.concept: A kernel supplies feature-space inner products without explicitly constructing every feature coordinate.
teaching.useWhen: Use it when a nonlinear geometry is useful but pairwise similarity is cheaper or clearer than explicit feature construction.
teaching.examMove: Check that the Gram matrix is positive semidefinite before treating a similarity function as a valid kernel.
teaching.trap: A visually plausible similarity is not automatically a valid kernel or a useful predictor.

math.explanation: The kernel value is the inner product of the inputs after the implicit feature map. A method can therefore use richer geometry without storing every transformed coordinate explicitly.
math.name: Kernel inner-product identity
math.purpose: Use it to work in an implicit feature geometry without explicitly constructing the transformed coordinates.

sections.title: Textbook depth · Do not conflate objectives
sections.body: PCA is not a clustering algorithm, and a high-variance direction is not automatically a predictive direction. Compare each method by its objective, output, and failure mode before choosing it for a dataset.

examples.title: Worked example: choose a method
steps: If the task is compressing ten correlated measurements into two coordinates, start with PCA.
If the task is assigning every point to exactly one of K groups, K-means matches that hard-assignment goal.
If points overlap and you need uncertainty such as $P(cluster 1 | x)$, use a probabilistic mixture such as a GMM.
examples.answer: Method choice follows the question: compression, hard grouping, or probabilistic membership.

math.explanation: A valid kernel gives the inner product that would be obtained after mapping inputs through $\phi$, without requiring us to build the transformed coordinates explicitly. The kernel changes the geometry available to a method such as a kernel SVM or kernel PCA.
math.name: Kernel inner-product identity
math.purpose: Use it to reason about an implicit feature map without constructing its coordinates explicitly.
math.caveat: A kernel is not automatically a probability or a distance; its role depends on the algorithm using it.

math.explanation: PCA evaluates how much centered data varies after projection onto a unit direction $v$. The covariance matrix stores pairwise feature variation; the quadratic form selects the variance visible along $v$.
math.name: Projected variance quadratic form
math.purpose: Use it to compute the variance visible along a unit PCA direction.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why does a high-variance direction not necessarily give the best predictive feature?
criticalQuestions.angle: Separate unsupervised reconstruction from supervised target information.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: PCA optimizes variance in $X$ without looking at $Y$. A low-variance direction can contain the signal that predicts the target, while a high-variance direction can be nuisance variation.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What must be true for a kernel matrix to represent a valid inner-product geometry?
criticalQuestions.angle: Think about symmetry and non-negative quadratic forms.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The Gram matrix should be symmetric positive semidefinite; otherwise the implicit inner-product interpretation breaks.
